# Standard library reference

<!-- GENERATED by `nsl doc stdlib` from stdlib/. Do not edit by hand: `cargo test -p nsl-cli` fails if this page and the sources differ. -->

Everything `stdlib/` declares: 26 modules, 47 free functions and 12 models. Signatures are rendered from the parser, so an entry here is what the compiler accepted, not what a comment claims. Descriptions come from `##` doc comments in the source (`#` is an ordinary comment and does not appear here); an item with no `##` block is listed with its signature alone, so the gaps are visible rather than hidden.

Most of NSL's numeric surface is *language*, not library: tensor arithmetic, `matmul`, `softmax`, `relu` and the rest are compiler builtins reached without an import. This page covers only what is written in NSL itself and imported with `from <module> import <name>`.

## `nsl.compat`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/compat.nsl`*

Interoperability with external ML frameworks — safetensors, HuggingFace
and ONNX.

The conversions themselves (`load_safetensors`, `save_safetensors`,
`from_hf`, `to_onnx`) are compiler intrinsics callable without importing
this module; what lives here is the shim-revision marker.

### `fn compat_version() -> int`

The compatibility-shim revision. Bumped when the shims below change
shape, so a program can branch on it.

## `nsl.data.loader`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/data/loader.nsl`*

Data loading and input pipelines.

The loading operations themselves (`DataLoader`, `load_jsonl`, `load_csv`,
…) are compiler intrinsics callable without importing this module; what
lives here is the version marker a program can branch on.

### `fn data_version() -> int`

The dataset-shim revision, bumped when the loader contract changes.

## `nsl.inference.generate`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/inference/generate.nsl`*

Autoregressive text generation.

### `@no_grad fn generate(lm, prompt: Tensor, max_tokens: int, temperature: float, top_k: int) -> Tensor`

Autoregressive generation: extend `prompt` by up to `max_tokens`,
sampling each step from `lm`'s logits with `temperature` and `top_k`
(`top_k = 1` is greedy decoding).

`lm` is any model whose `forward` maps a token tensor to logits.

## `nsl.inference.sampling`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/inference/sampling.nsl`*

Token sampling strategies for generation.

### `fn sample_top_k(logits: Tensor, k: int, temperature: float) -> Tensor`

Sample one token from the `k` highest-probability logits, after
dividing by `temperature`. Lower temperature concentrates the
distribution; `k = 1` is greedy.

### `fn sample_top_p(logits: Tensor, p: float, temperature: float) -> Tensor`

Nucleus sampling: sample from the smallest set of tokens whose
probabilities sum to at least `p`, after dividing by `temperature`.
Unlike top-k the candidate set resizes with the model's confidence.

### `fn sample_greedy(logits: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Take the single highest-probability token. Deterministic.

## `nsl.io`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/io.nsl`*

Console input.

### `fn input(prompt: str) -> str`

Print `prompt` and read one line from standard input, without the
trailing newline.

## `nsl.math`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/math.nsl`*

Scalar helpers that NSL does not provide as builtins.

The builtins cover tensor math; these are the `float` -> `float`
utilities a training script reaches for when computing a schedule or
clamping a hyper-parameter.

### `fn clamp(x: float, lo: float, hi: float) -> float`

Constrain `x` to `[lo, hi]`. Returns `lo` when `x < lo` and `hi` when
`x > hi`; `x` is returned unchanged in between.

The bounds are not checked. Given `lo > hi` the lower test wins:
every `x < lo` returns `lo` and everything else returns `hi`, so `x`
never comes back unchanged.

### `fn lerp(a: float, b: float, t: float) -> float`

Linear interpolation: `a` at `t = 0`, `b` at `t = 1`. `t` outside
`[0, 1]` extrapolates rather than clamping.

### `fn sign(x: float) -> float`

The sign of `x` as -1.0, 0.0 or 1.0. Exactly 0.0 maps to 0.0.

### `fn max_val(a: float, b: float) -> float`

The larger of `a` and `b`. Named `max_val` because `max` is a tensor
builtin.

### `fn min_val(a: float, b: float) -> float`

The smaller of `a` and `b`. Named `min_val` because `min` is a tensor
builtin.

## `nsl.nn.activations`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/nn/activations.nsl`*

Named wrappers over the activation builtins.

Each function here is a one-line forward to a compiler builtin of the
same shape. They exist so an activation can be passed by name and
imported like any other library item; calling the builtin directly is
equivalent and is what the compiler sees either way.

### `fn relu_act(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Rectified linear unit: `max(x, 0)`, elementwise.

### `fn gelu_act(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Gaussian Error Linear Unit, the activation used by the transformer MLP
in `nsl.nn.layers`.

### `fn silu_act(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Sigmoid Linear Unit (also called swish): `x * sigmoid(x)`.

### `fn sigmoid_act(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Logistic sigmoid, elementwise, into `(0, 1)`.

### `fn tanh_act(x: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Hyperbolic tangent, elementwise, into `(-1, 1)`.

### `fn softmax_act(x: Tensor, dim: int) -> Tensor`

Softmax along `dim`: exponentiate and normalise so that dimension sums
to 1. For a loss, prefer `nsl.nn.losses.cross_entropy`, which is
numerically stabler than softmax followed by a log.

## `nsl.nn.attention`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/nn/attention.nsl`*

Reference multi-head self-attention.

### `model Attention(dim: int, num_heads: int)`

Multi-head self-attention with a causal mask.

The reference formulation, written out in NSL: project to Q/K/V,
split into `num_heads` heads, scaled dot-product with a causal mask,
then recombine and project out. `nsl.nn.gqa` is the production form —
grouped-query, rotary, and fusible to a flash-attention kernel.

## `nsl.nn.gqa`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/nn/gqa.nsl`*

Grouped-query attention — the production attention block.

### `model GroupedQueryAttention(d_model: int, n_heads: int, n_kv_heads: int, head_dim: int, dropout_p: float, max_seq_len: int, rope_theta: float, n_layers: int)`

Grouped-query attention with rotary positions — the attention the
production models use.

`n_kv_heads` key/value heads are shared across `n_heads` query heads,
which cuts the KV cache by `n_heads / n_kv_heads` at inference.
Projections are Xavier-initialised and the output projection is
additionally scaled by `1/sqrt(2 * n_layers)` so residual variance
does not grow with depth.

`forward` takes a dense `[batch, seq, d_model]` batch. `forward_packed`
takes a packed batch with `segment_ids` and `position_ids`, so several
documents share a row without attending across the boundary.

#### `_n_kv_heads: Tensor`

#### `_head_dim: Tensor`

#### `_n_rep: Tensor`

#### `_dropout_p: Tensor`

## `nsl.nn.losses`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/nn/losses.nsl`*

Loss functions for training and distillation.

`mse_loss` / `l1_loss` / `bce_loss` are elementwise regressions;
`cross_entropy` is the classification loss the language-modeling head
uses, and honours -100 as an ignore index. `fused_linear_ce` and
`fused_kl_ce` are the fusible forms — written as ordinary composites
so they run anywhere, and recognised by codegen inside a decorated
`train`/`distill` block so the logits are never materialised.

### `fn mse_loss(pred: Tensor, target: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Mean squared error between `pred` and `target`, averaged over every
element. Both tensors must broadcast to a common shape.

### `fn l1_loss(pred: Tensor, target: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Mean absolute error between `pred` and `target`, averaged over every
element. Less sensitive to outliers than `mse_loss`.

### `fn cross_entropy(logits: Tensor, targets: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Softmax cross-entropy over `logits` `[N, C]` against integer class
`targets` `[N]`, averaged over the valid positions.

Targets of -100 are the ignore index: they are masked out of both the
numerator and the count, so padded positions in a packed batch do not
dilute the loss. Computed through `log_softmax`, so it is stable for
logits far from zero.

### `fn bce_loss(pred: Tensor, target: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Binary cross-entropy between probabilities `pred` and targets in
`[0, 1]`. `pred` is clamped away from 0 and 1 before the log, so a
saturated prediction costs a large finite loss rather than infinity.

### `fn fused_linear_ce(x: Tensor, W: Tensor, bias: Tensor, targets: Tensor) -> Tensor`

Fused linear + cross-entropy: the language-modeling head as one call.

    loss = fused_linear_ce(x, W, bias, targets)
          = cross_entropy(x @ W^T + bias, targets)

Shapes, matching the fused kernel's FFI:

    x:       [B*S, H]  f32   hidden states
    W:       [V,   H]  f32   LM head, row-major (transposed here)
    bias:    [V]       f32
    targets: [B*S]     i64   -100 = ignore index

Returns a scalar loss, the mean over valid positions. Written as the
explicit composite so it runs anywhere; inside a `train` block
decorated with `@fused_lm_ce(enabled = true)`, source-AD substitutes a
kernel that never materialises the `[B*S, V]` logits. The two paths are
the same function to the caller, including ignore-index semantics.

### `fn fused_kl_ce(x_s: Tensor, W_s: Tensor, bias_s: Tensor, x_t: Tensor, W_t: Tensor, bias_t: Tensor, targets: Tensor, alpha: float, temperature: float) -> Tensor`

Fused KL-CE distillation loss: hard-label CE plus a soft KL term.

    loss = alpha * CE(student_logits, targets)
         + (1 - alpha) * T^2 * KL(softmax(teacher/T) || softmax(student/T))

Shapes, matching the fused kernel's FFI:

    x_s:     [rows, HS]  f32   student hidden states
    W_s:     [V,    HS]  f32   student LM head, row-major
    bias_s:  [V]         f32
    x_t:     [rows, HT]  f32   teacher hidden states (frozen)
    W_t:     [V,    HT]  f32   teacher LM head (frozen)
    bias_t:  [V]         f32
    targets: [rows]      i64   -100 = ignore index

Returns a scalar loss, the mean over valid rows. The `T^2` factor keeps
the soft-target gradient scale independent of the temperature. Inside a
`distill` block decorated with `@fused_kl_ce(enabled = true, ...)`,
source-AD substitutes a kernel that materialises neither `[rows, V]`
logit tensor; `alpha` and `temperature` must then be numeric literals
at the call site, because the kernel takes them as compile-time
constants.

## `nsl.nn.rope`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/nn/rope.nsl`*

Rotary position embeddings.

### `fn rope_freq_table(dim: int, max_seq_len: int, theta: float) -> Tensor`

Build the `[max_seq_len, dim]` rotary frequency table that `cos`/`sin`
are taken over: row `p` is `concat(p * inv_freq, p * inv_freq)`.

A free function rather than a method because a model field
initializer cannot reference a sibling field, and both cached tables
plus `inv_freq` need the same derivation.

### `model RotaryEmbedding(dim: int, max_seq_len: int, theta: float)`

Rotary position embeddings (RoPE), applied to Q and K.

`cos`/`sin` are precomputed over the whole `[max_seq_len, dim]` grid
at construction and gathered per call, rather than rebuilt on every
attention layer. Consequently `seq_len` must not exceed
`max_seq_len`: the bound is enforced at the gather, which aborts
naming the offending index.

The `_`-prefixed fields are derived constants, not parameters — the
prefix keeps them out of the trainable set, so they take no gradient,
no optimizer moments and no weight decay.

#### `inv_freq: Tensor`

#### `_dim: Tensor`

#### `_half_dim: Tensor`

#### `_cos_table: Tensor`

#### `_sin_table: Tensor`

#### `fn forward(self, x: Tensor, seq_len: int) -> Tensor`

#### `fn forward_with_positions(self, x: Tensor, position_ids: Tensor) -> Tensor`

## `nsl.optim.adam`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/adam.nsl`*

Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2015).

`adam_step` below is byte-identical to `adamw_step`, and the decay it
applies is decoupled — it scales `param` directly rather than entering
the gradient as classical Adam's coupled L2 term.

The two names are NOT interchangeable, because only part of training
goes through this function. Under `grad_accumulation = 1` the compiler
calls it and `adam` and `adamw` behave the same. Under accumulation
greater than 1 the FASE path emits the update itself, and there
`adam` is compiled with **weight decay forced to zero** while `adamw`
applies it (`fase_optimizer.rs::emit_final_step`). Choosing `adam` for
an accumulating run therefore trains with no regularisation at all.

Prefer `nsl.optim.adamw` unless you specifically want no decay.

The moment buffers `m` and `v` are allocated by codegen and updated in
place through `copy_data`, so the step writes through its arguments
and returns nothing.

### `fn adam_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, m: Tensor, v: Tensor, lr: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, eps: float, weight_decay: float, t: float)`

One Adam step on `param`, in place. `m` and `v` are the first and
second moment buffers, bias-corrected with `t` (the 1-based step
number).

## `nsl.optim.adamw`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/adamw.nsl`*

AdamW: Adam with decoupled weight decay (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019).

The moment buffers `m` and `v` are allocated by codegen and updated in
place through `copy_data`, so the step writes through its arguments and
returns nothing.

### `fn adamw_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, m: Tensor, v: Tensor, lr: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, eps: float, weight_decay: float, t: float)`

One AdamW step on `param`, in place.

`m` and `v` are the first and second moment buffers, bias-corrected
with `t` (the 1-based step number). Decay is *decoupled*: it scales
`param` directly rather than entering the gradient, so it does not
interact with the second-moment normalisation.

`nsl.optim.adam`'s step function is byte-identical to this one, but the
two optimizer NAMES diverge under gradient accumulation — see
`nsl.optim.adam`.

## `nsl.optim.lion`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/lion.nsl`*

Lion (EvoLved Sign Momentum; Chen et al., 2023): the update is the
SIGN of an interpolated momentum, so every parameter moves by the same
magnitude and only one state buffer is needed.

That buffer (`m`) is allocated by codegen and updated in place through
`copy_data`, so the step writes through its arguments and returns
nothing.

### `fn lion_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, m: Tensor, lr: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, weight_decay: float)`

One Lion step on `param`, in place.

The update direction uses `beta1` to blend momentum with the current
gradient; `m` is then updated with the usually-larger `beta2`. Because
the step is a sign, Lion wants a learning rate roughly 3-10x smaller
than AdamW's at the same model scale.

## `nsl.optim.muon`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/muon.nsl`*

Muon: momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schulz, with AdamW routing.

The orthogonalized update applies only to rank-2 hidden weight matrices;
embeddings, the LM head and every non-rank-2 tensor take an AdamW step.

### `fn muon_orthogonalize(g: Tensor, ns_steps: float) -> Tensor`

Approximate the semi-orthogonal factor `UV^T` of `g`'s SVD by a
quintic Newton-Schulz iteration of `ns_steps` steps.

The coefficients are Jordan et al.'s slope-maximizing tuning, so
singular values converge into a band around 1 rather than exactly
1. A tall input is orthogonalized through its transpose, keeping
the Gram matrix at the smaller dimension.

This is the pinned REFERENCE implementation the gates compare
against; `muon_step` calls the runtime primitive instead, which is
the same math without the per-iteration device sync.

### `fn muon_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, m: Tensor, v: Tensor, adamw_route: float, lr: float, adamw_lr: float, momentum: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, eps: float, weight_decay: float, nesterov: bool, ns_steps: float, t: float)`

One Muon step on `param`, in place, with mixed AdamW routing.

`adamw_route` selects the update per parameter: the orthogonalized-
momentum step applies only to rank-2 hidden weight matrices, while
embeddings, the LM head and anything whose runtime rank is not 2
(biases, norms, scalars) take a standard AdamW step. Codegen sets
the flag from parameter roles, so a caller does not classify by
hand.

`m` is the Muon momentum buffer on the Muon route and AdamW's first
moment otherwise; `v` is allocated only for AdamW-routed parameters
and is not read on the Muon route. The Newton-Schulz iteration runs
in the tensor's native dtype — there is no bf16 shortcut.

## `nsl.optim.schedulers`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/schedulers.nsl`*

Learning-rate schedules: `(base_lr, step, ...) -> lr`.

Each is a pure function of the step number, so a schedule can be
evaluated anywhere without carrying optimizer state, and two
schedules can be compared by plotting them.

### `fn constant_lr(base_lr: float, step: float) -> float`

A flat schedule: `base_lr` at every step. The null control for a
schedule comparison.

### `fn step_lr(base_lr: float, step: float, step_size: float, gamma: float) -> float`

Staircase decay: multiply by `gamma` every `step_size` steps.

### `fn exponential_lr(base_lr: float, step: float, gamma: float) -> float`

Smooth exponential decay: `base_lr * gamma**step`, per step (not per
epoch), so `gamma` is typically very close to 1.

### `fn linear_decay(base_lr: float, step: float, total_steps: float, end_factor: float) -> float`

Straight line from `base_lr` at step 0 to `base_lr * end_factor` at
`total_steps`, then flat.

### `fn cosine_anneal(base_lr: float, step: float, t_max: float, eta_min: float) -> float`

Cosine curve from `base_lr` down to `eta_min` over `t_max` steps,
flat at `eta_min` afterwards. No warmup — see `warmup_cosine`.

### `fn warmup_cosine(base_lr: float, step: float, warmup_steps: float, total_steps: float, min_lr: float) -> float`

Linear warmup for `warmup_steps`, then cosine decay to `min_lr` at
`total_steps`. The schedule production recipes use.

`total_steps` is the horizon the cosine is shaped to, NOT a step
cap: a run stopped at a fraction of it has only travelled that
fraction of the curve, so a schedule copied from a long run into a
short one holds the rate near its peak throughout. Size
`total_steps` to the run you are actually doing.

### `fn one_cycle(base_lr: float, step: float, max_lr: float, total_steps: float, pct_start: float) -> float`

One-cycle (Smith, 2018): linear rise from `base_lr` to `max_lr` over
the first `pct_start` of `total_steps`, then a cosine fall to zero.

## `nsl.optim.sgd`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/sgd.nsl`*

Stochastic gradient descent with momentum, dampening, decoupled weight
decay and optional Nesterov lookahead.

The single state buffer (`velocity`) is allocated by codegen and
updated in place through `copy_data`, so the step writes through its
arguments and returns nothing.

### `fn sgd_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, velocity: Tensor, lr: float, momentum: float, dampening: float, weight_decay: float, nesterov: bool)`

One SGD step on `param`, in place.

`velocity` carries the momentum buffer. `dampening` scales the
incoming gradient's contribution to it; `nesterov` applies the
lookahead form, which uses the gradient plus the *updated* velocity
rather than the velocity alone.

## `nsl.optim.soap`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/optim/soap.nsl`*

SOAP (Vyas et al., 2024), diagonal form.

State buffers are allocated by codegen and written in place.

### `fn soap_step(param: Tensor, gradient: Tensor, m: Tensor, v: Tensor, lr: float, beta1: float, beta2: float, eps: float, t: float)`

One SOAP step on `param`, in place.

This is the diagonal-preconditioner form: the moment update and
bias correction are Adam's, without the decoupled decay term. The
Shampoo-style eigenbasis rotation SOAP is named for is not
implemented here.

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/peft.nsl`*

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning surface.

### `model WrgaAdapter()`

The marker base a custom WRGA adapter conceptually attaches to.

Importing it is the intent marker; the WRGA compiler pass keys off
the `@wrga(adapter = <Name>, ...)` decorator, not off this type.

## `nsl.quant.ops`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/quant/ops.nsl`*

Quantization entry points.

### `fn quantize(t: Tensor, dtype: str, granularity: str, axis: int, group_size: int) -> QuantizedTensor`

Quantize `t` to `dtype` (`"int8"`, `"int4"`, `"fp8_e4m3"`, …).

`granularity` selects the scale's scope — per tensor, per `axis`, or
per group of `group_size` elements along it. Finer granularity costs
more scale storage and recovers more accuracy.

### `fn dequantize(qt: QuantizedTensor) -> Tensor`

Reconstruct a float tensor from `qt`, applying its stored scales.
Lossy: this does not recover the pre-quantization values.

## `nsl.tokenize.tokenizer`

*Source: `stdlib/nsl/tokenize/tokenizer.nsl`*

Tokenizer handles.

A tokenizer is referred to by an integer handle rather than a value,
so it can be created once and shared across a dataset pipeline.

### `fn create_byte_tokenizer() -> int`

Create a byte-level tokenizer (256 vocabulary entries, no training
needed) and return its handle.

### `fn encode(tok: int, text: str) -> Tensor`

Encode `text` to a tensor of token ids using tokenizer `tok`.

### `fn decode(tok: int, ids: Tensor) -> str`

Decode a tensor of token `ids` back to text using tokenizer `tok`.

### `fn vocab_size(tok: int) -> int`

The number of entries in `tok`'s vocabulary.

### `fn save(tok: int, path: str)`

Serialize tokenizer `tok` to `path`.

### `fn load(path: str) -> int`

Load a tokenizer from `path` and return its handle.
